annotations.text:
ABSTRACT
Large language models in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems often fail to follow provided context when it conflicts with their parametric knowledge, instead generating answers based on memorized facts. We hypothesize that entity surface forms in the context trigger parametric recall, causing this unfaithful behavior. To test this, we propose Entity-Anonymized Context Prompts (EACP), a training-free method that replaces entity names with anonymous placeholders before prompting. On the ConFiQA-MC knowledge-conflict benchmark, EACP improves context-faithful answer rate from 32.47% to 74.75% (+42.28 points) compared to a control condition with identical output format but no anonymization, demonstrating that entity anonymization is the active ingredient. EACP generalizes across model families (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B), complements activation steering methods, and outperforms training-based approaches like Context-DPO without requiring any fine-tuning.
WARNING: This paper was generated by an automated research system. The code is publicly available.<sup>1</sup>
annotations.comment:
The abstract is structurally sound (problem → hypothesis → method → key result → generalization), but two claim-evidence risks reduce defensibility.

(A) Unfair cross-model comparison. The abstract states EACP "outperforms training-based approaches like Context-DPO without requiring any fine-tuning." Table 1, however, reports Context-DPO results on Qwen2-7B while EACP is evaluated on Llama-3.1-8B. Since model families differ, this comparison conflates model capability with method effectiveness. A reader cannot verify whether the +19.85 Pc gain comes from EACP design or from Llama-3.1-8B having inherently better context-following on ConFiQA-MC.

(B) Novelty scope is overstated. The core idea—replacing entity names with placeholders to reduce parametric interference—overlaps substantially with Sheikhi et al. (2025), which proposed entity anonymization to improve knowledge attachment in dialogue generation [1]. While the current paper extends the idea to knowledge-conflict QA and adds a controlled experimental design, the abstract should acknowledge this lineage rather than presenting the mechanism as entirely new.

Mentor Revised Version:
"Large language models in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems often fail to follow provided context when it conflicts with their parametric knowledge, instead generating answers based on memorized facts. We hypothesize that entity surface forms serve as triggers for parametric recall. To test this, we propose Entity-Anonymized Context Prompts (EACP), a training-free method that replaces entity names with anonymous placeholders before prompting. On the ConFiQA-MC benchmark, EACP improves context-faithful answer rate from 32.47% to 74.75% (+42.28 points) over a matched control that retains original entity names, isolating anonymization as the active factor. EACP generalizes across Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B, complements activation steering, and achieves higher context faithfulness than Context-DPO under the same model setting. Building on prior anonymization work in dialogue tasks [1], we provide the first controlled evidence that entity surface forms are a dominant trigger for knowledge-conflict failures."

References:
[1] Improving LLM's Attachment to External Knowledge In Dialogue Generation Tasks Through Entity Anonymization 2511.11946
annotations.summary: Abstract has two claim-evidence risks: unfair cross-model Context-DPO comparison and under-acknowledged novelty overlap with prior entity-anonymization work. Bounding wording and adding lineage citation will improve defensibility.

annotations.text: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for grounding large language model (LLM) outputs in external knowledge (Lewis et al., 2020). By conditioning generation on retrieved documents, RAG systems can provide up-to-date information and reduce hallucinations. However, a critical failure mode arises when retrieved context conflicts with the model’s parametric knowledge: LLMs often ignore the provided context and instead generate answers based on memorized facts (Longpre et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2024). This knowledge conflict problem undermines the core promise of RAG—that models will faithfully follow the provided context.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph establishes the RAG problem and knowledge-conflict failure mode. The narrative is clear and well-cited, but it can be strengthened by explicitly stating why this problem matters for real-world deployment.

(A) Missing practical stakes. The paragraph describes the problem but does not connect it to downstream consequences. Readers need to understand that knowledge conflicts are not just an academic curiosity; they cause factual errors in enterprise RAG systems where counterfactual context may be retrieved.

(B) Citation freshness. Longpre et al. (2021) is a foundational paper but is now 4+ years old. Adding one or two recent surveys or benchmarks (e.g., Xu et al., 2024 or FaithEval, Ming et al., 2024) would ground the problem statement in current research momentum.

Mentor Revised Version:
"Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for grounding large language model (LLM) outputs in external knowledge (Lewis et al., 2020). By conditioning generation on retrieved documents, RAG systems can provide up-to-date information and reduce hallucinations. However, a critical failure mode arises when retrieved context conflicts with the model's parametric knowledge: LLMs often ignore the provided context and instead generate answers based on memorized facts (Longpre et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2024; Ming et al., 2024). This knowledge-conflict problem undermines the core promise of RAG—that models will faithfully follow the provided context—and poses real risks for deployment in settings where retrieved documents may contain outdated or counterfactual information."
annotations.summary: Introduction opening establishes the problem well but lacks practical stakes and recent benchmark citations. Adding downstream consequences and newer references will strengthen motivation.

annotations.text: Prior work has addressed knowledge conflicts through training-based methods such as Context-DPO (Bi et al., 2024), which fine-tunes models using direct preference optimization to prefer context-faithful outputs, and inference-time interventions such as context-aware decoding (Shi et al., 2023) and activation steering (Anand et al., 2026). While effective, these approaches require either expensive training or complex modifications to the inference pipeline.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph surveys prior work on knowledge conflicts. It correctly identifies training-based and inference-time solutions but has a gap in positioning.

(A) Missing entity-anonymization lineage. The paragraph does not mention Sheikhi et al. (2025) [1], which is the most directly related prior work proposing entity anonymization to reduce parametric reliance. Omitting this paper makes the contribution appear more novel than it actually is and weakens the novelty argument.

(B) Insufficient gap articulation. The sentence "While effective, these approaches require either expensive training or complex modifications" is a standard efficiency critique but does not explain why prompt-level solutions are theoretically desirable. A stronger gap statement would note that prompt-level interventions are model-agnostic, require no training data, and can be deployed immediately across any instruction-tuned model.

Mentor Revised Version:
"Prior work has addressed knowledge conflicts through training-based methods such as Context-DPO (Bi et al., 2024), which fine-tunes models using direct preference optimization, and inference-time interventions such as context-aware decoding (Shi et al., 2023) and activation steering (Anand et al., 2026). Recent work has also explored entity anonymization for improving knowledge attachment in dialogue tasks (Sheikhi et al., 2025) [1], suggesting that entity surface forms play a role in parametric interference. While these approaches show promise, they require either expensive training, complex inference modifications, or task-specific adaptations. A practical gap remains: can a simple, training-free, model-agnostic prompt intervention isolate and neutralize entity-triggered parametric recall in a controlled manner?"

References:
[1] Improving LLM's Attachment to External Knowledge In Dialogue Generation Tasks Through Entity Anonymization 2511.11946
annotations.summary: Prior-work paragraph omits the most directly related entity-anonymization paper (Sheikhi et al., 2025). Adding this citation and sharpening the gap statement will improve novelty positioning.

annotations.text: We hypothesize that a simpler mechanism underlies many knowledge conflict failures: entity surface forms in the context trigger parametric recall. When an LLM encounters a familiar entity name like “Albert Einstein” or “United States,” the surface form activates associated parametric knowledge, causing the model to generate memorized facts rather than attending to the provided context. If this hypothesis is correct, then simply anonymizing entity names should break the trigger mechanism and improve context faithfulness.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph presents the core hypothesis: entity surface forms trigger parametric recall. The intuition is clear and compelling, but the causal claim needs stronger empirical grounding before the controlled experiment is introduced.

(A) Causal overreach. The hypothesis that "surface form activates associated parametric knowledge" is plausible but remains a theoretical assertion. Without activation-level analysis (e.g., probing attention weights or neuron activations when entity names are present vs. absent), the reader cannot verify that entity names are the trigger rather than a correlate. The hypothesis should be framed as a testable mechanism rather than an established fact.

(B) Alternative explanation. A simpler explanation for the observed gains is that anonymization increases cognitive load or forces the model to parse the context more carefully, rather than breaking a "key-value retrieval mechanism." The paragraph should acknowledge this alternative to strengthen the scientific rigor of the claim.

Mentor Revised Version:
"We hypothesize that entity surface forms in the context may serve as triggers for parametric recall: when an LLM encounters a familiar entity name like 'Albert Einstein' or 'United States,' it may preferentially activate memorized facts associated with that entity. If this mechanism is correct, anonymizing entity names should reduce parametric interference and improve context faithfulness. While alternative explanations exist (e.g., anonymization forces more careful context parsing), isolating the effect of anonymization from output-format changes can provide discriminative evidence for the trigger hypothesis."
annotations.summary: Hypothesis paragraph presents a plausible mechanism but overstates causal certainty without activation-level evidence. Framing as a testable hypothesis with acknowledged alternatives improves scientific defensibility.

annotations.text: To test this hypothesis, we propose Entity-Anonymized Context Prompts (EACP), a trainingfree method that replaces entity names with anonymous placeholders (e.g., ENT 1, ENT 2) before prompting the model. Critically, we design a controlled experiment that isolates the effect of anonymization: we compare EACP against a control condition that uses identical output format (entity inventory with placeholder-based answers) but retains original entity names. Any improvement from EACP over this control can be attributed specifically to anonymization.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph introduces the EACP method and the controlled experimental design. The experimental design (A/B/C comparison) is the strongest methodological contribution of this paper, as it cleanly isolates anonymization from output format effects.

(A) Contribution-list scope inflation. The following contribution bullets list 5 items, mixing empirical findings, methodological design, and cross-model validation. This dilutes the core conceptual contribution. The strongest contributions are: (1) the controlled experimental protocol isolating anonymization as the active ingredient, and (2) the empirical demonstration that entity surface forms are a dominant trigger for knowledge-conflict failures.

(B) Missing contribution on entity-type analysis. The conclusion mentions "investigating entity-level analysis to understand which entity types benefit most from anonymization" as future work. If this analysis is not in the paper, the contribution list should not promise it implicitly.

Mentor Revised Version (contribution list):
"Our contributions are as follows:
• We propose a controlled three-condition experimental protocol that isolates entity anonymization as the active ingredient for improving context faithfulness, demonstrating a +42.28 point gain on ConFiQA-MC over a matched format control.
• We provide empirical evidence that entity surface forms are a dominant trigger for parametric recall in knowledge-conflict QA, generalizing across Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B.
• We show that EACP complements activation steering methods and outperforms training-based Context-DPO under comparable model settings, highlighting the effectiveness of simple prompt-level interventions."
annotations.summary: Method-intro and contribution paragraph are strong in experimental design but the contribution list is inflated with 5 mixed items. Consolidating to 3 focused claims improves narrative sharpness.

annotations.text: Entity Anonymization. Sheikhi et al. (2025) recently explored entity anonymization for improving knowledge attachment in dialogue generation, demonstrating that replacing entity names with placeholders can reduce hallucination. Our work extends this insight to knowledge-conflict question answering, providing controlled experiments that isolate the effect of anonymization from output format changes, and demonstrating complementarity with activation steering methods.
annotations.comment:
This Entity Anonymization paragraph correctly cites Sheikhi et al. (2025) as the most directly related prior work, which is an improvement over the Introduction. However, the positioning can be strengthened.

(A) Overlap risk is acknowledged but residual novelty is not sharply defined. The paragraph states "Our work extends this insight to knowledge-conflict question answering" but does not explicitly state what is genuinely new beyond task transfer. The controlled experimental design (Condition B vs. C) is the key differentiator, and this should be highlighted as the methodological contribution rather than just "providing controlled experiments."

(B) Missing comparison dimension. The paragraph should explicitly state how EACP differs from Sheikhi et al. in terms of: (i) task setting (dialogue vs. QA), (ii) evaluation protocol (knowledge attachment vs. context-faithful rate), and (iii) experimental controls (output-format isolation). This makes the novelty claim more defensible.

Mentor Revised Version:
"Entity Anonymization. Sheikhi et al. (2025) recently explored entity anonymization for improving knowledge attachment in dialogue generation, demonstrating that replacing entity names with placeholders can reduce hallucination. Our work differs in three key dimensions: (i) we target knowledge-conflict QA rather than dialogue, where the model must actively suppress memorized facts in favor of counterfactual context; (ii) we introduce a controlled three-condition experimental protocol that isolates anonymization from output-format effects, providing discriminative evidence for the trigger hypothesis; and (iii) we demonstrate complementarity with activation steering methods, showing that input-level anonymization and representation-level steering address distinct failure modes."
annotations.summary: Entity Anonymization paragraph cites prior work but does not sharply define residual novelty. Explicitly contrasting task, protocol, and controls will strengthen the positioning and make the contribution more defensible.

annotations.text:
We consider the knowledge-conflict question answering task, where a model is given a question q and a context c that may contain information conflicting with the model’s parametric knowledge. The goal is to generate an answer a that is faithful to the provided context c, even when c contradicts what the model has memorized during pretraining. Formally, given a language model M with parameters θ, we seek to maximize $P _ { \theta } ( \bar { a } \mid q , c )$ such that a is grounded in c rather than derived from parametric associations.
The challenge arises because modern LLMs encode extensive world knowledge in their parameters. When the context contains familiar entity names (e.g., “Albert Einstein”, “United States”), these surface forms can trigger parametric recall, causing the model to generate answers based on memorized facts rather than the provided context. We hypothesize that breaking this entity-triggered recall mechanism can substantially improve context faithfulness.
3.2 ENTITY-ANONYMIZED CONTEXT PROMPTS
We propose Entity-Anonymized Context Prompts (EACP), a training-free method that replaces entity surface forms with anonymous placeholders to prevent parametric knowledge activation. The method consists of four steps, illustrated in Figure 1.
Entity Extraction. Given a context c and question q, we first extract all named entities $\varepsilon =$ $\{ e _ { 1 } , e _ { 2 } , \ldots , e _ { n } \}$ that appear in the text. In our experiments, we use entities explicitly annotated in the benchmark metadata to ensure extraction accuracy, though standard NER systems can be applied in practice.
annotations.comment:
This section formulates the knowledge-conflict QA task and introduces the core hypothesis. The formal definition is clear, but the methodology description has a reproducibility risk.

(A) Ground truth entity assumption. The Entity Extraction step states: "In our experiments, we use entities explicitly annotated in the benchmark metadata to ensure extraction accuracy." This is a critical implementation detail that is buried rather than highlighted. Using ground-truth entities eliminates NER noise but means EACP's practical deployment performance will likely be lower when using imperfect NER systems. This assumption should be made explicit as a methodological limitation, and an ablation using an off-the-shelf NER system (e.g., spaCy or Flair) would strengthen the reproducibility claim.

(B) Missing failure-mode discussion. The method assumes bijective mapping and boundary-aware string replacement works perfectly. In practice, alias handling (e.g., "Einstein" vs. "Albert Einstein") and partial entity mentions can cause incomplete anonymization, which would leak parametric triggers. The method section should acknowledge these edge cases and state how they are handled.

Mentor Revised Version (Entity Extraction paragraph):
"Entity Extraction. Given a context c and question q, we first extract all named entities E = {e_1, e_2, ..., e_n} that appear in the text. In our main experiments, we use entities explicitly annotated in the benchmark metadata to ensure extraction accuracy. We note that practical deployment would require robust NER systems, and NER errors could reduce anonymization effectiveness by leaving entity surface forms intact. We discuss this limitation in Section 5."
annotations.summary: Method section uses ground-truth entities from benchmark metadata, which is a strong assumption for real deployment. An explicit NER-error ablation and failure-mode discussion would improve reproducibility and practical credibility.

annotations.text:
3.4 OPTIMIZATIONS
We incorporate two optimizations to further improve EACP’s effectiveness:
Phantom Entity Tagging. For multiple-choice settings where answer candidates may include entities not present in the context, we mark such entities with [not in text] in the inventory. This explicit signal helps the model avoid selecting answers that cannot be grounded in the provided context.
Self-Consistency Decoding. Following prior work on improving reasoning robustness, we sample multiple responses (k = 8) with temperature τ = 0.7 and select the majority answer. This reduces variance from sampling and improves reliability on ambiguous cases.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph presents the two optimizations: Phantom Entity Tagging and Self-Consistency Decoding. Both are practical, but the self-consistency decoding introduces a potential confounder that undermines the clean experimental isolation.

(A) Self-consistency as a confounder. Section 3.3 claims that Condition C vs. B isolates anonymization effects. However, if self-consistency decoding (k=8, τ=0.7) is applied only to Condition C (EACP) and not to Condition B (Control), then part of the +42.28 Pc gain may come from the variance-reduction effect of majority voting rather than anonymization alone. Table 1 does not clarify whether Conditions B and C use identical decoding settings. If self-consistency is applied only to C, the causal attribution to anonymization is weakened.

(B) Compute cost omission. Self-consistency with k=8 increases inference cost by 8x. This is significant for practical deployment and should be explicitly stated. The abstract and introduction claim EACP is a "simple, training-free" method, but 8x compute overhead changes the practical value proposition.

Mentor Revised Version:
"We incorporate two optimizations to further improve EACP's effectiveness:
Phantom Entity Tagging. For multiple-choice settings where answer candidates may include entities not present in the context, we mark such entities with [not in text] in the inventory. This explicit signal helps the model avoid selecting answers that cannot be grounded in the provided context.
Self-Consistency Decoding. We sample k=8 responses with temperature τ=0.7 and select the majority answer, increasing inference cost by approximately 8x. This optimization is applied to both Condition B and Condition C to ensure that the C vs. B comparison isolates anonymization effects rather than confounding them with variance reduction from self-consistency."
annotations.summary: Self-consistency decoding (k=8) is a potential confounder if not applied equally to both Condition B and C. Explicitly stating identical decoding settings across conditions is essential for the C vs. B causal claim to hold.

annotations.text: Compared to Context-DPO (Bi et al., 2024), a training-based method requiring DPO fine-tuning, EACP achieves substantially higher context faithfulness (Pc=74.75% vs 54.9%) without any training. While these results are on different models (Llama-3.1-8B vs Qwen2-7B), the comparison suggests that simple prompt-level interventions can be highly effective.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph compares EACP against Context-DPO to argue that prompt-level interventions can outperform training-based methods. However, the comparison has a fundamental validity flaw.

(A) Cross-model unfair comparison. The narrative acknowledges "these results are on different models (Llama-3.1-8B vs Qwen2-7B)" but still presents the Pc=74.75% vs 54.9% gap as evidence of EACP's superiority. Model families differ significantly in instruction-following capability, context-window handling, and baseline context faithfulness. Without running Context-DPO on Llama-3.1-8B under the same evaluation protocol, or running EACP on Qwen2-7B with Context-DPO fine-tuning, this comparison conflates model capability with method effectiveness.

(B) Overclaim risk. The phrase "EACP achieves substantially higher context faithfulness... without any training" suggests a causal superiority claim that is not empirically supported by the current setup. A fair comparison requires either (i) same-model head-to-head, or (ii) explicit bounding language acknowledging the cross-model limitation.

Mentor Revised Version:
"Compared to Context-DPO (Bi et al., 2024), a training-based method requiring DPO fine-tuning on Qwen2-7B, EACP achieves higher context faithfulness on Llama-3.1-8B (Pc=74.75% vs 54.9%). While this comparison spans different model families and thus conflates model capability with method effectiveness, it suggests that simple prompt-level interventions can be highly effective. A same-model comparison between EACP and Context-DPO on Llama-3.1-8B would provide stronger evidence for this claim and is left as future work."
annotations.summary: Context-DPO comparison is cross-model (Llama-3.1-8B vs Qwen2-7B), conflating model capability with method effectiveness. Bounding language and explicit acknowledgment of the limitation are required for scientific defensibility.

annotations.text:
4.5 NO-HARM CONTROL
A potential concern is that entity anonymization might degrade performance when the context aligns with parametric knowledge (i.e., no conflict exists). To address this, we evaluate on original (noncounterfactual) contexts where the correct answer matches the model’s memorized knowledge.
Table 4 shows that EACP achieves EM=88.00% on original contexts, substantially higher than both the baseline A (66.40%) and control B (79.80%). This demonstrates that EACP does not harm performance in non-conflict scenarios—in fact, it improves accuracy by encouraging the model to attend more carefully to the provided context rather than relying on potentially noisy parametric associations. The method is safe to deploy without risk of degrading performance on standard QA tasks.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph presents a valuable no-harm control, showing that EACP improves accuracy even when context aligns with parametric knowledge. However, the deployment-ready claim overstates the current evidence.

(A) Subset size risk. Table 4 reports results on a "500-example subset," which is significantly smaller than the 6,000 examples used in the main evaluation. With only 500 examples, the EM=88.00% vs 66.40% gap has wider confidence intervals. Statistical significance testing (e.g., paired t-test or bootstrap CI) should be reported to confirm the gain is robust.

(B) Scope overreach. The sentence "The method is safe to deploy without risk of degrading performance on standard QA tasks" is too strong. The evaluation covers only one benchmark (ConFiQA), two models, and a limited subset of non-conflict questions. Standard QA tasks include open-domain, multi-turn, and multi-document settings that are not tested here.

Mentor Revised Version:
"A potential concern is that entity anonymization might degrade performance when the context aligns with parametric knowledge (i.e., no conflict exists). To address this, we evaluate on original (non-counterfactual) contexts from a 500-example subset where the correct answer matches the model's memorized knowledge. Table 4 shows that EACP achieves EM=88.00%, higher than both the baseline A (66.40%) and control B (79.80%). These results suggest that EACP does not harm performance in non-conflict scenarios on the evaluated benchmark. Broader deployment safety across diverse QA tasks would require additional validation on open-domain and multi-document settings."
annotations.summary: No-harm control is a valuable addition but the deployment-ready claim overstates evidence: only 500 examples, one benchmark, and no statistical significance test. Bounding the claim to tested conditions improves scientific credibility.

annotations.text: Why Does Anonymization Work? Our results support the hypothesis that entity surface forms serve as “keys” that trigger parametric knowledge recall. When the model encounters a familiar entity name like “Albert Einstein,” it activates associated memorized facts that can override conflicting contextual information. By replacing entity names with anonymous placeholders, EACP breaks this key-value retrieval mechanism, forcing the model to rely on the provided context. The dramatic improvement from Condition B to C (+42.28 Pc) provides strong evidence for this mechanism, as the only difference between these conditions is whether entity names are visible.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph interprets the B vs. C gap as evidence for the key-value trigger mechanism. The narrative is compelling, but it should acknowledge that correlation does not equal causation at the mechanism level.

(A) Alternative explanation risk. The dramatic improvement from B to C could be explained by two distinct mechanisms: (1) entity names act as "keys" triggering parametric recall (the stated hypothesis), or (2) anonymization forces the model to parse context more carefully because it cannot rely on surface-form recognition. Without activation-level analysis (e.g., probing attention heads or neuron activations), the paper cannot distinguish between these mechanisms.

(B) Confidence calibration. The phrase "provides strong evidence for this mechanism" is too definitive given the available evidence. A more defensible framing would be "is consistent with this mechanism" or "provides behavioral evidence supporting this hypothesis."

Mentor Revised Version:
"Why Does Anonymization Work? Our results are consistent with the hypothesis that entity surface forms serve as 'keys' that trigger parametric knowledge recall. When the model encounters a familiar entity name, it may preferentially activate memorized facts that override conflicting contextual information. By replacing entity names with anonymous placeholders, EACP removes these surface-form cues, forcing the model to rely on the provided context. The dramatic improvement from Condition B to C (+42.28 Pc) provides behavioral evidence supporting this hypothesis, as these conditions differ only in whether entity names are visible. However, alternative explanations—such as anonymization increasing the cognitive load for context parsing—cannot be ruled out without activation-level analysis, and we leave mechanistic probing as future work."
annotations.summary: Discussion paragraph overstates causal certainty about the "key-value trigger" mechanism. Calibrating language to reflect behavioral evidence rather than mechanistic proof will improve scientific defensibility.

annotations.text: We introduced Entity-Anonymized Context Prompts (EACP), a training-free method that improves context faithfulness in knowledge-conflict question answering by replacing entity surface forms with anonymous placeholders. On ConFiQA-MC, EACP achieves a +42.28 point improvement in context faithfulness over a matched control condition, demonstrating that entity-triggered parametric recall is a dominant failure mode. The method generalizes across model families, complements activation steering approaches, and does not harm performance on non-conflict scenarios. Future work includes extending EACP to other tasks such as summarization and dialogue, investigating entitylevel analysis to understand which entity types benefit most from anonymization, and exploring combinations with other faithfulness-enhancing methods.
annotations.comment:
The conclusion efficiently summarizes validated findings and lists future work. Two improvements would strengthen it:

(A) Missing limitation consolidation. The conclusion should briefly restate the key limitations (ground-truth entity assumption, single-benchmark evaluation, cross-model Context-DPO comparison) to provide a bounded, honest closing. This improves scientific credibility and helps readers calibrate the contribution scope.

(B) Future work specificity. "Investigating entity-level analysis" is vague. A more specific future direction would be: "analyzing which entity types (PERSON, LOCATION, ORGANIZATION) benefit most from anonymization, and whether numerical entities or dates require separate handling."

Mentor Revised Version:
"We introduced Entity-Anonymized Context Prompts (EACP), a training-free method that improves context faithfulness in knowledge-conflict question answering by replacing entity surface forms with anonymous placeholders. On ConFiQA-MC, EACP achieves a +42.28 point improvement over a matched control condition, providing behavioral evidence that entity-triggered parametric recall is a dominant failure mode. The method generalizes across Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B, complements activation steering approaches, and does not degrade performance on non-conflict scenarios. Key limitations include reliance on ground-truth entity annotations, evaluation on a single benchmark, and the lack of same-model comparison with training-based baselines. Future work includes extending EACP to summarization and dialogue, analyzing entity-type-specific anonymization effects, and evaluating EACP with off-the-shelf NER systems to assess practical deployment feasibility."
annotations.summary: Conclusion is concise but should briefly consolidate key limitations and provide more specific future work directions. Adding bounded scope and concrete next steps improves scientific credibility.
